questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer with rolled edges on his right hand that developed after a thorn prick. Gram stain shows Gram-positive rods in chains. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Bacillus anthracis causes cutaneous anthrax presenting as a painless papule that ulcerates into an eschar with surrounding oedema. Gram-positive rods in chains (bamboo cane appearance) are characteristic. Farmers/animal handlers are at risk.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis, and pathergy test positivity. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Behcet's disease (International Study Group criteria) requires recurrent oral ulcers plus two of: genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions, positive pathergy test. Pathergy (skin hyperreactivity to minor trauma) is especially common in Middle Eastern and Asian patients.

questions.q: A 22-year-old sexually active male presents with painless inguinal lymphadenopathy and a groove sign (inguinal and femoral nodes separated by Poupart's ligament). The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: The groove sign (genitoinguinal groove created by enlarged nodes above and below Poupart's ligament) is pathognomonic of Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. The primary lesion is often small and heals before lymphadenopathy appears.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man from a leprosy-endemic area develops sudden erythema and swelling of existing skin lesions, fever, and painful nerve involvement over 2 days. The bacillary index is high. This reaction is best classified as:
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL/Type 2 reaction) occurs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It is an immune complex-mediated reaction (Type III hypersensitivity). Features include tender nodules, systemic symptoms (fever, malaise), and high bacillary load. Type 1 (reversal) occurs across the borderline spectrum.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with tense bullae on erythematous skin predominantly on the trunk and flexures. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid typically presents in elderly patients with tense bullae on erythematous or normal skin. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ (hemidesmosomes — BP180/230 antigens). Pemphigus shows intercellular IgG (fish-net pattern). Dermatitis herpetiformis shows granular IgA at dermal papillae.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules on her wrists with lacy white lines on the surface. Similar lesions are seen on the buccal mucosa. The pathological hallmark on histology is:
opts: Saw-tooth rete ridges with vacuolar degeneration of basal layer
questions.exp: Lichen planus histology shows: hyperkeratosis, irregular acanthosis with saw-tooth rete ridges, vacuolar degeneration (liquefaction) of basal cell layer, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ, and colloid/Civatte bodies (apoptotic keratinocytes). Wickham's striae on mucosa are pathognomonic.

questions.q: A 25-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 150 cells/µL) presents with hundreds of pearly umbilicated papules all over the face and trunk that have been enlarging for 3 months. The best treatment for widespread molluscum contagiosum in this setting is:
opts: Antiretroviral therapy to restore immune function
questions.exp: In HIV-infected patients, giant/widespread molluscum contagiosum reflects severe immunosuppression (usually CD4 <200). The definitive treatment is restoration of immune function through antiretroviral therapy (ART). Physical ablation treats individual lesions but recurrences are inevitable without immune recovery. Acyclovir is not active against molluscum (a poxvirus).

questions.q: A 45-year-old diabetic man presents with black eschar on the nose and palate with periorbital oedema and proptosis after a bout of diabetic ketoacidosis. KOH mount shows broad aseptate hyphae. The most appropriate antifungal is:
questions.exp: Rhinocerebral mucormycosis (caused by Mucor, Rhizopus, Absidia — Order Mucorales) presents in diabetic/immunocompromised patients. KOH shows broad, ribbon-like, aseptate/pauci-septate hyphae. Treatment requires surgical debridement + liposomal Amphotericin B. Voriconazole has NO activity against Mucorales.

questions.q: A 20-year-old student presents with annular scaly patches on the scalp with broken hair shafts (black dots). KOH shows endothrix infection. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.exp: Endothrix tinea capitis (black dot ringworm) is caused by Trichophyton species (T. violaceum, T. tonsurans, T. soudanense). Spores fill the hair shaft without an ectothrix sheath. Microsporum canis causes large-spore ectothrix. Epidermophyton does not infect hair.

questions.q: A 60-year-old farmer presents with a warty plaque on the dorsum of the foot with black dots (Medlar bodies) on histology. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis presents as verrucous plaques on exposed sites. Histology shows Medlar bodies (sclerotic bodies, copper-penny bodies) — brown, thick-walled, round cells with cross-septation, pathognomonic. Causes: Fonsecaea pedrosoi (most common), Cladophialophora carrionii, Phialophora verrucosa.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and arthritis. ANA is positive (1:640). Anti-dsDNA titre is elevated. The cutaneous finding most specific for SLE is:
questions.exp: Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) plaques — scarring, follicular plugging, atrophy, hyperpigmented borders — are highly specific for lupus. Malar rash (butterfly rash) is more sensitive but less specific. Gottron's papules are specific for dermatomyositis, not SLE.

questions.q: A 48-year-old man presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, skin tightening proximal to MCP joints, bilateral interstitial lung fibrosis, and positive anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I). This antibody is associated with:
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) and carries higher risk of pulmonary fibrosis and renal crisis. Anti-centromere antibodies (ACA) are associated with limited cutaneous SSc/CREST. Anti-U1-RNP with MCTD.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, and proximal muscle weakness. Skin biopsy shows interface dermatitis. The most common internal malignancy associated with this condition in adults is:
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis in adults has a strong paraneoplastic association. In women, ovarian carcinoma is the most commonly associated malignancy. Overall, the risk of malignancy is 15–30% in adult dermatomyositis. MDA-5 antibody is associated with amyopathic dermatomyositis and ILD.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along a dermatome, preceded by burning pain for 2 days. Which antiviral should be started within 72 hours for best efficacy?
questions.exp: Herpes zoster is treated with valacyclovir 1 g TDS for 7 days (or acyclovir 800 mg 5×/day for 7 days, or famciclovir 500 mg TDS for 7 days). Valacyclovir achieves higher bioavailability and simpler dosing. Treatment within 72 hours reduces duration and prevents post-herpetic neuralgia.

questions.q: A neonate at day 3 of life develops crusted lesions around the mouth and nares. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. The most appropriate management is:
questions.exp: Neonatal herpes simplex (HSV) is a life-threatening emergency. IV acyclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours for 14-21 days is the standard of care for all neonatal HSV (cutaneous, CNS, or disseminated). Oral agents are inadequate for neonates due to absorption variability and severity of disease.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with an enlarging pearly nodule with rolled, translucent borders, telangiectases on the surface, and central ulceration on the nose. The most common histological subtype of this tumour is:
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer. Nodular BCC is the most common histological subtype (~60-70%), presenting as the classic pearly papule/nodule with rolled borders, telangiectases, and central ulceration (rodent ulcer). Morphoeic BCC has the worst prognosis due to ill-defined margins.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man with a history of extensive sun exposure presents with a rapidly growing keratinous nodule with a central keratin-filled crater that partially resolved spontaneously over 3 months. This is most likely:
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) is a rapidly growing, self-limited epithelial tumour arising from hair follicle. Classic presentation: rapid growth over 4-6 weeks, volcano-like nodule with central keratin plug, spontaneous involution over 3-6 months. Histologically resembles well-differentiated SCC; some consider KA a low-grade SCC variant.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with an asymmetric, multicoloured (brown, black, red, white) pigmented lesion with irregular borders on the back measuring 8 mm. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network, regression structures, and blue-white veil. The next best step is:
questions.exp: Suspected melanoma should undergo excisional biopsy (complete excision with 1-2 mm margins) to allow accurate Breslow thickness measurement, which determines prognosis and re-excision margins. Shave biopsy is contraindicated as it may transect the lesion and invalidate staging. Punch biopsy is acceptable only when excisional biopsy is not feasible.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with unilateral hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on the face. Slit skin smear is negative. Skin biopsy shows granulomas along nerve bundles with epithelioid cells and no AFB. Classification as per Ridley-Jopling scale:
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) presents with 1-3 well-defined, hypopigmented, anaesthetic patches with raised edges, absent sweat/hair. Biopsy shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas that may invade and destroy nerve bundles, with rare/absent AFB (paucibacillary). Ridley-Jopling spectrum: TT-BT-BB-BL-LL.

questions.q: A 25-year-old with multibacillary leprosy develops a sudden acute tender nodular eruption on the face, trunk, and extremities with fever and arthralgia after starting dapsone. The most appropriate immediate treatment is:
questions.exp: Thalidomide is the drug of choice for ENL (Type 2 lepra reaction) due to its anti-TNF-α mechanism. Dose: 100-400 mg/day. Prednisolone is an alternative, especially when thalidomide is contraindicated (women of childbearing age due to teratogenicity). Clofazimine has anti-inflammatory properties but takes weeks to work.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with fragile skin, blistering at sites of minor trauma on the dorsum of hands, hyperpigmentation, and hypertrichosis. Urine shows pink fluorescence under Wood's lamp. The enzyme deficiency responsible is:
questions.exp: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is caused by deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) leading to accumulation of uroporphyrins. Features: photosensitivity, skin fragility, blistering on exposed areas, hypertrichosis, hyperpigmentation, sclerodermoid changes. Urine/stool shows uroporphyrins (pink-red fluorescence). Triggers: alcohol, iron, hepatitis C, oestrogens.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with perioral and acral dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhoea. She has been exclusively breastfeeding her infant and reports poor dietary intake. Plasma zinc level is undetectable. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an autosomal recessive disorder of zinc absorption (SLC39A4 mutation). Classic triad: acral/periorificial dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhoea. Acquired zinc deficiency can mimic it. Treatment: oral zinc supplementation (zinc sulfate 1-3 mg/kg/day). Necrolytic migratory erythema is associated with glucagonoma.

questions.q: A patch test is being performed for contact dermatitis investigation. The reading at 48 hours shows erythema, oedema, and vesicles. At 96 hours the reaction has intensified. This pattern is most consistent with:
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction. Patch test reactions in ACD intensify from 48 to 96 hours (crescendo pattern). Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) reactions are maximal at 48 hours and fade by 96-120 hours (decrescendo). ACD requires prior sensitisation; ICD does not.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with known atopic dermatitis develops widespread eczematous eruption with fever after using a topical steroid for herpes labialis. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Eczema herpeticum (Kaposi varicelliform eruption) occurs when HSV-1 (less commonly HSV-2 or VZV) superinfects atopic dermatitis or other inflammatory skin conditions. Topical steroids suppress local immunity, promoting viral spread. Presents with punched-out erosions/vesicles on eczematous skin, fever, and lymphadenopathy. Treatment: systemic acyclovir.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with recurrent painful oral ulcers, skin lesions described as target lesions, and conjunctival involvement. He took sulfonamides 2 weeks ago. The pathomechanism of this condition involves:
opts: Drug-reactive cytotoxic T cells targeting keratinocytes
Immune complex deposition in vessel walls
Direct toxic effect of drug metabolites on keratinocytes
questions.exp: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) is primarily mediated by drug-specific cytotoxic CD8+ T cells (and NK cells) that target and destroy keratinocytes via granulysin, perforin/granzyme pathways, and FasL-Fas interaction. HLA associations (e.g., HLA-B*57:01 for abacavir) guide pharmacogenomic screening.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman on methotrexate for psoriasis develops megaloblastic anaemia and mouth ulcers. Methotrexate exerts its anti-psoriatic effect primarily by:
opts: Inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase leading to reduced T cell proliferation
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocking tetrahydrofolate synthesis, which inhibits DNA synthesis and T-lymphocyte proliferation (key in psoriasis pathogenesis). It also promotes adenosine release (anti-inflammatory). Folic acid supplementation reduces mucosal/haematological side effects without compromising efficacy. MTX requires monitoring of LFTs and CBC.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with hypopigmented macules on the trunk, upper back, and arms that show yellowish-green fluorescence under Wood's lamp. KOH mount shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (and related species). KOH mount shows hyphae and round spores ('spaghetti and meatballs'/'banana and grapes'). Wood's lamp: yellowish-green/golden fluorescence. Hypopigmentation due to azelaic acid inhibiting melanogenesis. Treatment: topical selenium sulfide, azoles, or single-dose oral fluconazole.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with bilateral symmetrical hyperpigmentation over sun-exposed areas of face, neck (Casal's necklace), hands, and forearms with glossitis, diarrhoea, and dementia. The deficiency responsible is:
questions.exp: Pellagra is caused by niacin (vitamin B3/nicotinic acid) deficiency or tryptophan deficiency. Classic 4D's: Dermatitis (photosensitive, Casal's necklace), Diarrhoea, Dementia, Death. The hyperpigmented scaling rash on sun-exposed areas is pathognomonic. Associated with maize-based diets, alcoholism, carcinoid syndrome, Hartnup disease, and isoniazid use.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with palpable purpura on the lower legs, haematuria, and elevated ESR. Skin biopsy shows leucocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits on DIF. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura, HSP) is characterised by palpable purpura (usually lower limbs/buttocks), arthralgia, GI involvement, and renal disease (IgA nephropathy). DIF shows perivascular IgA deposits — this is the diagnostic hallmark distinguishing it from other leucocytoclastic vasculitides.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man undergoes Mohs micrographic surgery for a facial BCC. The principal advantage of this technique over standard excision is:
opts: It allows frozen section of the entire specimen
Complete margin assessment with maximum tissue conservation
It is faster than wide local excision
It does not require a pathologist
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) achieves the highest cure rates for BCC/SCC (99% for primary BCC) by processing tissue horizontally, allowing 100% margin assessment while conserving maximum normal tissue. Standard WLE samples only 1-2% of margins. MMS is preferred for high-risk tumours, recurrent lesions, and cosmetically sensitive areas.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with diffuse hair loss 3 months after a severe febrile illness. Trichoscopy shows an increased percentage of club hairs. Hair pull test is positive with telogen bulbs. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Telogen effluvium (TE) is caused by premature shift of anagen follicles to telogen phase due to triggers (fever, surgery, childbirth, crash dieting, hypothyroidism). It presents 2-4 months after the trigger with diffuse hair shedding. Hair pull test positive with club (telogen) hairs. Usually self-limiting in 6-12 months after trigger removal. Anagen effluvium follows chemotherapy with proximal hair shaft fractures.
